purpose: Verify that Cost Override changes the actual optimal recovery decision, not only the UI value: default costs favor delay recovery, while a deliberately low cancellation penalty favors cancelling the complete disrupted E1 rotation.
manual_checks: With canonical phase2_test_v1 costs, the disrupted E1 rotation is recovered by F101 +60 and F102 +20; the schedule cost is 80.
With only flight_cancellation overridden from 25000 to 20, the E1 rotation flips to three cancellations; the schedule cost is 60.
The unaffected E2 control rotation remains original in both variants.
No aircraft/crew reassignment, ferry, deadhead, or passenger effect is needed in either variant.
The decision flip is therefore attributable to the cost override rather than a different scenario, capacity profile, or algorithm profile.
design_notes: This Case intentionally tests an integrated rotation-level delay-versus-cancel tradeoff instead of pretending a cancelled first leg is independent of aircraft/crew terminal continuity.
The two bundles are identical except for cost_overrides.flight_cancellation, making the causal test explicit.
The override value 20 is deliberately synthetic and exists only to force a deterministic regression decision flip; it is not a business-calibrated cancellation cost.
Default comparison: delay recovery costs 60 + 20 = 80, while cancelling the three-leg E1 cycle costs 3 x 25000 = 75000.
Override comparison: cancelling the three-leg E1 cycle costs 3 x 20 = 60, lower than the unchanged 80 delay-recovery cost.
